stem: A nurse participates in care planning for an adult with type 2 diabetes. Which approach to specialty referral best reflects current diabetes standards?

options.A: Arrange referrals according to the client’s complications, comorbidities, treatment complexity, and individual needs rather than assuming every client with diabetes requires the same specialist.
options.B: Refer every adult with diabetes to endocrinology at diagnosis because specialty care is universally required regardless of clinical needs.
options.C: Use a single hemoglobin A1C value as a universal rule that automatically determines whether endocrinology referral is required.
options.D: Avoid specialty referral once diabetes is diagnosed because primary care alone should manage all diabetes-related complications.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care emphasize individualized, team-based diabetes care and recommend specialist referrals as appropriate for complications, comorbidities, treatment burden, and other person-specific needs. The standards do not establish one universal endocrinology referral threshold for every adult with type 2 diabetes, nor do they require endocrinology referral for every diagnosis. B and C impose unsupported universal rules. D is incorrect because diabetes-related complications often require collaboration with appropriate specialists such as endocrinology, nephrology, cardiology, ophthalmology, podiatry, behavioral health, or other professionals depending on the clinical problem.
educational_objective: Coordinate diabetes specialty referrals according to the client’s actual complications, comorbidities, treatment complexity, and support needs rather than applying a universal referral rule or laboratory cutoff.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Improving Care and Promoting Health in Populations: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Section 1 team-based care table — individuals with diabetes-related complications or comorbidities: specialist referrals as appropriate and available; Section 4 treatment planning — referral to diabetes education and medical specialists as needed; additional referrals arranged as necessary according to complications, comorbidities, and treatment burden
source_claim_supported: Current ADA standards support individualized specialist referral based on complications, comorbidities, treatment burden, and client needs rather than a universal endocrinology referral requirement or single A1C cutoff.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; coordinate referrals and collaborate with interprofessional team members based on client needs
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized specialty referral in diabetes
correction_summary: Rejected the source item’s unsupported claim that specific ‘common endocrinology referral criteria’ are established by ADA. The final item tests the current standards-based principle of individualized interprofessional referral according to complications, comorbidities, treatment complexity, and client needs, without inventing a universal A1C threshold.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sections 1 and 4. The standards use individualized ‘as appropriate/as needed’ specialist referral language. A 2026 ADA meeting abstract specifically notes the absence of established guidelines for referral of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes to endocrinology, reinforcing that the source item’s purported fixed criteria should not be presented as an ADA rule.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A mirrors the current standards without converting flexible referral planning into a mandatory universal algorithm. No numeric A1C cutoff is asserted.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; specialist involvement is individualized to clinical needs and complexity.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; endocrinology referral is not universally required for every adult diabetes diagnosis.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; the cited standards do not establish a single A1C value as a universal endocrinology-referral trigger.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; appropriate specialty referral is explicitly part of comprehensive diabetes care when complications or needs warrant it.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A preserves the person-centered, complication-based referral framework; B-D impose absolute rules contradicted by current standards.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address referral strategy at the same level of abstraction.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is directly appropriate because the construct is coordination of interprofessional specialty services.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether ADA provides universal endocrinology referral criteria, distinction between general specialist referral and endocrinology specifically, A1C-cutoff overprecision, team-based care language, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
